2012 / Latin America / Packaging

Front-of-Package Food Warning Labels

Across Latin America, food warning labels have become one of the clearest examples of communication design used as part of public health policies. In addition to the use of small nutrition tables, or technical nutrition data, these “Excess Sugar,” “Excess Sodium,” “Excess Calories,” or “Excess Saturated Fats” labels are prominently placed on the front of food and beverage packaging.

The warning label system follows a similar approach to tobacco warning labels, giving buyers an immediate, high-contrast message that is hard to overlook, before purchase. In doing so, it makes hidden health risks easier to recognize, simplifying the need to read a more complex nutrition guide table, making these more accessible to a wider population.

These graphics have been in use in Latin America, starting in Chile in 2012, and rolled out in other countries, help educate people about cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and certain types of cancer, leading causes of death in the Region, all linked to unhealthy diets and the high consumption of ultra-processed and processed foods with high levels of sugars, fats, and sodium.

From an SD Standard perspective, this project shows how visual communication can improve health and safety, reduce information inequality, and support more accountable product design. Its strength is not only the graphic form of the black octagon, resembling a stop sign, but the larger system behind it: nutrition thresholds, policy and regulatory enforcement, public education, and packaging redesign.

The project also demonstrates a “better project pattern” for designers: when communication affects public well-being, clarity should take priority over persuasion. A successful package is not only one that sells the product, but one that helps people understand the consequences of choosing it.

Criteria

  • EIRT7 / EnvironmentDurability & Extended Life

    The product or system is physically durable and has a longer life than the industry average, where desirable. The product or system can be reused, recharged, repaired, and/or upgraded as an environmental benefit.

  • EIRT8 / EnvironmentDurability & Extended Life

    The product or system is physically durable and has a longer life than the industry average, where desirable. The product or system can be reused, recharged, repaired, and/or upgraded as an environmental benefit.

  • EW2 / EnvironmentRecyclability or Reusability

    Materials or systems used increase the ease and likelihood of recycling and/or reuse of the product and its packaging.

  • CCP3 / CultureLocal Culture

    The project adapts to local and regional cultures.

  • CCE1 / CultureAudience Engagement

    The project engages end users throughout the design process or audiences that will be directly impacted by the project.

  • FFS2 / FinanceProfitability

    The project budget or contract financially compensates the design entity.

  • E2 / EnvironmentProduct Ingredients Transparency

    The project includes a list of all components and/or ingredients.

  • S2 / SocietyHealth and Safety

    The project improves the health or safety of the target audience.
